paragraphs.heading: What an enzyme is
paragraphs.text: An enzyme is a large biological molecule, usually a protein, that works as a catalyst: it speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up. The molecules it acts on are called substrates, and it turns them into products. Almost every metabolic process in a cell needs enzymes to run fast enough to be useful to life. A metabolic pathway is usually a chain of steps, each one handled by an enzyme. Enzymes are known to drive more than 5,000 types of biochemical reaction.

paragraphs.heading: How they speed things up
paragraphs.text: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering what is called the activation energy, often by factors of millions. One enzyme, orotidine 5′-phosphate decarboxylase, makes a reaction that would otherwise take millions of years happen in milliseconds. Like any catalyst, an enzyme does not change the overall equilibrium of a reaction. It comes out restored at the end of each cycle, ready to work again.

paragraphs.heading: Picky and sensitive
paragraphs.text: What sets enzymes apart is how specific they are, which comes from each one's unique three-dimensional structure. They are also sensitive to conditions such as temperature and pH. Activators can raise their activity and inhibitors can lower it, and many of these substances serve as drugs or poisons. Outside the conditions that suit them, enzymes can lose their structure, a change called denaturation, and stop working.

paragraphs.heading: Enzymes at work for people
paragraphs.text: Enzymes have many practical uses. Industry uses them to help make antibiotics and other complex molecules. Biological washing powders contain enzymes that break down stains made of protein, starch and fat. Meat tenderizers use papain and similar protein-cutting enzymes to break down proteins, improving the texture of meat and making it easier to digest.

paragraphs.heading: From ferments to enzymes
paragraphs.text: By the late 1600s and early 1700s, people knew that stomach juices digest meat and that saliva and plant extracts turn starch into sugar, but not how. In 1833 the French chemist Anselme Payen discovered the first enzyme, diastase. Decades later Louis Pasteur studied how yeast ferments sugar into alcohol. He concluded that a vital force inside living yeast cells, called ferments, was responsible. In 1877 Wilhelm Kühne first used the word enzyme, from an Ancient Greek word meaning leavened, or in yeast.

paragraphs.heading: No living cells needed
paragraphs.text: In 1897 Eduard Buchner submitted his first paper on yeast extracts. In experiments at the University of Berlin he showed that sugar still fermented when no living yeast cells were present, and he named the enzyme responsible zymase. This discovery of cell-free fermentation won him the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Following his lead, enzymes are usually named by adding -ase to the substrate or the type of reaction, so lactase is the enzyme that cleaves lactose.

paragraphs.heading: Proteins after all
paragraphs.text: In the early 1900s nobody yet knew what enzymes were chemically. Many scientists linked their activity to proteins, while others, such as Richard Willstätter, argued that proteins only carried the true enzymes. John Howard Northrop and Wendell Meredith Stanley settled it through work on the digestive enzymes pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin, showing that pure proteins can be enzymes. They were among three scientists given the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Later, crystallized enzymes let researchers solve their structures by x-ray crystallography, first for lysozyme in 1965, which began the field of structural biology.
